opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Leo, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. Fair warning, I've got strong feelings about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's already a lie for people like me. "Handy tool" is what they call it while it eats my commissions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if nothing else changes, my work is already gone. Clients who used to pay me for a cover now type a prompt and pay me to fix the hands. For a third of the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the fix-up jobs I hate, keep posting my own work, and pick up bar shifts. I won't touch the generators. That's a line for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the generators. Even if it meant more work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then. They were trained on my art without asking. Using them would be helping someone rob me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bitter. Even the calm version isn't calm for me.

S0.say: "Handy tool" is what they call it while it eats my commissions.
S0.think: His work is already gone: clients prompt an image and pay him a third to fix it.
S0.do: Takes fix-up jobs he hates, keeps posting his own work, picks up bar shifts, and refuses to use generators.
S0.feel: Bitter, even the calm version isn't calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's theft, slow or fast. They scraped millions of artists' work without asking and now they're selling it back to our clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners hired means studios stop taking on juniors like me. I already can't get a staff job. Slow just means a slow death for anyone without a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Join the artists' class action groups, push for opt-out and pay for training data. Keep the bar shifts. Maybe teach a drawing class if a community centre will have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Furious and kind of worn out.

S1.say: It's theft, slow or fast. They scraped artists' work without asking and sell it back to our clients.
S1.think: Studios hiring fewer juniors means a slow death for artists like him without a name.
S1.do: Joins artists' legal action groups, campaigns for pay for training data, keeps bar shifts and looks for a teaching class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say welcome to our world. Artists were the warning. Now maybe office people will listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's grim, but I'd feel less alone. My work's still gone, though. And more laid-off people chasing the bar and café shifts I live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show up at every protest and union meeting going. Fight for whatever bill puts a tax on the AI firms. Hold onto the bar job tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, with a tiny bit of hope that people finally get it.

S2.say: Welcome to our world. Artists were the warning; maybe office people will listen now.
S2.think: Less alone, but his work is still gone and more laid-off people are chasing the shifts he lives on.
S2.do: Goes to protests and union meetings, backs taxes on AI firms, and holds tight to his bar job.
S2.feel: Angry, with a little hope people finally get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains belong to everyone whose work they were built on. That means a basic income, public ownership, all of it. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much. I'm already at the bottom. If anything, a political crisis is the only chance things get fixed. But I'd be skint, and rent would go up with house prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work as many bar and warehouse shifts as I can get. Physical stuff at least pays. Organise with other artists. Move back in with my mum if rent goes up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared about money, but fired up.

S3.say: The gains belong to everyone whose work AI was built on: basic income, public ownership, all of it.
S3.think: He's already at the bottom, and a political crisis may be the only chance of a fix, but rising rents would leave him broke.
S3.do: Works as many bar and warehouse shifts as possible, organises with other artists, and might move back in with his mum.
S3.feel: Scared about money, but fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they've taken the art, the office jobs, and now the bar and the warehouse. What's left? Who is this for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That was my backup. The physical jobs were where I was going to hide while I made art on the side. If robots take those, I have nothing. No savings, no family money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the last one you sounded almost hopeful about the crisis. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In that one, there was still somewhere for me to stand while we fought. In this one there isn't. Hope's hard on an empty stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Apply for whatever support exists. Squeeze into my mum's place. Keep drawing, because it's the only thing that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like the walls are closing in.

S4.say: They've taken the art, the office jobs, and now the bar and the warehouse. Who is this for?
S4.think: Physical jobs were his hiding place while he made art; without them he has nothing, with no savings or family money.
S4.do: Doesn't know; would apply for any support, move in with his mum, and keep drawing.
